final_qi.question: Is Mucolipidosis type I classified as a lysosomal storage disease?
final_qi.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I—also known as sialidosis—is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase (NEU1). The enzymatic defect leads to intralysosomal accumulation of sialyl-oligosaccharides and related substrates, producing the typical clinical and pathological features of a lysosomal storage disorder. Accordingly, it is universally grouped with other lysosomal storage diseases in standard medical genetics and metabolic-disease classifications.

final_qi.question: Is glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) classified as a lysosomal storage disease?
final_qi.long_answer: Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) results from inherited deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid α-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase). Because the metabolic defect is located in a lysosomal hydrolase and leads to intralysosomal accumulation of undegraded substrate (glycogen), it meets the defining criteria for a lysosomal storage disorder. In textbooks and authoritative reviews, Pompe disease is routinely listed alongside Gaucher, Fabry, Niemann-Pick, and other classic lysosomal storage diseases. Therefore, the classification of glycogen storage disease type II as a lysosomal storage disease is scientifically correct and consistent with established biomedical consensus.
